Ketchup sauces and breaded cutlets, plus the typical kissaten kitchen, mean there is no gluten-free menu and no celiac-safe preparation. Not suitable for those who must strictly avoid gluten.
nara_takarajima.vegan_detail: The menu centers on egg (omurice), pork cutlet, and chicken/meat-based Western dishes; coffee and dairy-based drinks and coffee jelly round it out. No vegan or vegetarian items are documented, and the signature dishes rely on egg, butter, and meat. Not a vegan-friendly destination.
nara_takarajima.notes: [Mom & Pop] Takarajima is a longtime retro kissaten tucked along the Shimogomon shopping street in Naramachi, a short walk from Kintetsu Nara Station. It has been quietly serving the neighborhood for over twenty years, run by an older proprietor who keeps oldies and jazz playing through a ca

chef_bio.background: Takarajima is a longtime retro kissaten tucked along the Shimogomon shopping street in Naramachi, about a ten-minute walk from Kintetsu Nara Station. It has been quietly serving the neighborhood for over twenty years, run by an older proprietor with a passion for music who keeps oldies and jazz playing through a calm, time-stopped interior decorated in classic Showa-era café style.
chef_bio.philosophy: An unhurried, nostalgic refuge: the owner curates the music and the slow pace as much as the food, the kind of neighborhood spot regulars return to for comfort rather than novelty.
chef_bio.specialty: Old-fashioned omurice — butter-scented ketchup chicken rice wrapped in a soft omelet — is the signature, most often ordered as a set with a small pork cutlet or curry. Lunch sets come with salad and a post-meal coffee or tea, and the house coffee and coffee jelly are local favorites.

anecdotes.text: Reviewers describe a nostalgic jazz-café ambiance with oldies flowing through a 'fallen-out-of-time' room, and praise the butter-scented, ketchup-laced old-style omurice (often as a pork-cutlet set) as the dish to order.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Tabelog reviews confirm a 20+ year Shimogomon-arcade kissaten run by an older, music-loving male proprietor, with oldies/jazz and a calm Showa 'time-stopped' room, whose signature is butter-scented ketchup omurice (pork-cutlet-and-omurice set ~1,200 yen with salad, coffee and coffee jelly).

gf_cross_contamination.text: Core dishes (omurice, breaded pork cutlet, curry) are flour- and wheat-based and prepared in a shared kissaten kitchen; no gluten-free handling is documented.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Signature items rely on egg, butter, and meat, with no vegan options noted; vegan diners cannot be reliably accommodated.

cultural_comfort.note: A quiet, longtime local kissaten where the menu and atmosphere are entirely Japanese — knowing how to order an omurice or cutlet set in basic Japanese will make the visit smooth, and cash is essential.

nara_kyoya.gf_detail: Udon is the house specialty and is made from wheat, and tempura batter and soy-based seasonings add further gluten. There is no gluten-free menu or documented accommodation, so this is not suitable for celiac diners.
nara_kyoya.vegan_detail: This is a fish-and-meat-forward Japanese eatery: udon broth, sashimi, tempura and chicken dishes all rely on fish dashi or animal ingredients. No vegan or vegetarian menu is documented, and even the udon sets are not plant-based.
nara_kyoya.notes: [Mom & Pop] Kyoya began as an udon specialist on Nishi-Kitsutsuji before relocating into a traditional wooden townhouse in Nara's atmospheric Naramachi quarter, a short walk from Kintetsu Nara Station near Sarusawa Pond. After the move it broadened from a pure udon shop into a full Japanese

chef_bio.background: Kyoya began as an udon specialist on Nishi-Kitsutsuji before relocating into a traditional wooden townhouse in Nara's atmospheric Naramachi quarter, a short walk from Kintetsu Nara Station near Sarusawa Pond. After the move it broadened from a pure udon shop into a full Japanese kitchen while keeping the smooth, springy noodles that built its name. By day it is a calm, casual lunch spot; in the evening it shifts into an izakaya mood.
chef_bio.specialty: Hand-served udon (bukkake and kama-age styles) with smooth, throat-pleasing noodles, plus the changing Kyoya Gozen lunch set that pairs udon with seasonal fish tempura, small side dishes, rice and pickles. Evening favorites include fresh sashimi platters, grilled chicken, and eggplant dengaku.

anecdotes.text: Diners describe the converted townhouse as a hidden-gem retreat, with shoes-off sunken-hearth seating downstairs and quiet tatami rooms upstairs giving an old-fashioned, peaceful feel.
The kitchen carried over the silky, pleasing udon texture from its original udon-shop days even after expanding the menu in Naramachi.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Nara-gourmet and narameshi confirm Kyoya's origin as a well-known Nishi-Kitsutsuji udon shop that moved to a Naramachi townhouse and expanded into a broader Japanese/izakaya menu (bukkake and kama-age udon, Kyoya Gozen set with fish tempura, evening sashimi/grilled chicken/eggplant dengaku), with sunken-hearth and upstairs tatami seating.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat udon is the central dish and tempura is fried on site, so wheat is pervasive in the kitchen.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Dishes such as bukkake udon, eggplant dengaku and grilled chicken use Japanese soy-based seasonings, which typically contain wheat.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Udon broth and most sets rely on fish dashi, and sashimi and chicken are prepared in the same kitchen.

cultural_comfort.note: A relaxed, homey local spot where you remove your shoes for tatami/hearth seating; staff are warm but communication is mostly in Japanese, so a few basic phrases or a translation app will help.

nara_someya_shoten.gf_detail: Not a gluten-free destination. The signature dashi-maki tamago and set meals rely on Japanese dashi and seasonings that typically include wheat-based soy sauce, and rice is served alongside. No gluten-free protocols are documented, so a celiac diner would need to ask directly and exercise caution.
nara_someya_shoten.vegan_detail: Not vegan-suitable. The core offering is egg-based (dashi-maki tamago, egg sandwiches, omurice) and the dashi is made from bonito (katsuo) and kombu, so it contains fish. No vegan options are documented.
nara_someya_shoten.hours_raw: 11:00-15:00 (L.O. 14:15), open daily including holidays; closes when sold out. Hours have varied across sources (one local report lists 10:30-18:00, closed Wednesdays). Closures are irregular — check before visiting.
nara_someya_shoten.notes: [Mom & Pop] Someya Shoten began about 70 years ago as a specialist workshop making thick-rolled egg for the sushi trade. Founder and master craftsman Masahiro Someya, now in his 80s, supplied gyoku (sushi-topping egg) and sweet datemaki egg rolls wholesale to fish markets and sushi restauran

chef_bio.background: Someya Shoten began about 70 years ago as a specialist workshop making thick-rolled egg for the sushi trade. Founder and master craftsman Masahiro Someya, now in his 80s, supplied gyoku (sushi-topping egg) and sweet datemaki egg rolls wholesale to fish markets and sushi restaurants. As the family workshop's members aged past 70 and questions of succession and physical strain set in, the family decided to preserve the craft in a new form, converting the ground floor of their three-story former workshop-residence in Naramachi into a small cafe one summer.
chef_bio.philosophy: The founder's eldest daughter Kiyoko, who now runs the cafe, describes the aim that customers remember their dashi-maki tamago so warmly they would want to taste it one more time. Ingredients are sourced locally: eggs, Koshihikari rice, Yamato (Nara) vegetables, and domestic bonito and kombu for the broth.
chef_bio.specialty: Dashi-maki tamago (dashi-rolled omelet) teishoku set meals; also a thick egg sandwich and classic omurice. The signature omelet is built around about four eggs and a generous amount of dashi for a soft, fluffy texture, cooked fresh to order.

anecdotes.text: The founder said he wanted to make the decision to wind down the original factory while he was still physically able to handle disposing of the large machinery.
The cafe occupies the converted first floor of the family's former three-story workshop-residence in Naramachi, and the dashi-maki tamago is prepared fresh for each order.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Nara.keizai.biz reports founder Masahiro Someya (81) ran a ~70-year gyoku/datemaki egg workshop wholesaling to sushi shops; with the family aging past 70 he converted the ground floor of the three-story workshop-residence into a cafe, now run by eldest daughter Kiyoko. Dashi-maki set ~800 yen uses about four eggs with abundant dashi; local Koshihikari, Yamato vegetables, domestic bonito/kombu.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Set meals and the dashi-based omelet use traditional Japanese seasonings; soy sauce in Japan is typically wheat-containing, and no gluten-free soy sauce is documented here.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The kitchen centers entirely on egg dishes and uses fish (bonito) and kombu dashi, so animal products are pervasive throughout the menu.

positives.text: Ingredients are simple and locally sourced: local eggs, Koshihikari rice, Nara vegetables, and domestic bonito and kombu broth.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny family-run spot in an old house with a one-order-per-person and no-reservations policy; a little Japanese and patience help, as this is a traditional local eatery rather than a tourist-oriented restaurant.

nara_yanagi_chaya.gf_detail: No gluten-free program is documented. The signature warabi mochi is made from bracken starch (warabiko), which is wheat-free at its base, but the shop is a traditional sweets house with no published allergen handling and no dedicated preparation for celiacs. Matcha and Japanese sweets are generally low-wheat, but the savory side (奈良茶飯 / nara chameshi sets, often accompanied by pickles and side dishes) and any soy-sauce-based seasonings are not verified gluten-free. A celiac diner must ask directly; cross-contact cannot be assumed safe.
nara_yanagi_chaya.vegan_detail: No vegan menu is documented. Warabi mochi (bracken starch, sugar, kinako soy flour) can be plant-based, but the kinako/anko and matcha sweets may involve dairy in some variations (e.g., the milk warabi mochi version), and savory dishes such as 奈良茶飯 are not confirmed dashi-free. Vegan-leaning diners should ask which sweets are free of dairy; this is not a dedicated vegetarian/vegan destination.
nara_yanagi_chaya.hours_raw: 11:30-17:00 (L.O. 16:30); some listings note Wed/Thu opening at 11:00. Closed Mondays.
nara_yanagi_chaya.notes: [Mom & Pop] Yanagi Chaya was founded in 1902 (Meiji 35) beside Sarusawa Pond, in the shadow of Kofukuji's five-story pagoda in central Nara. It was opened specifically to keep alive Nara's old tea-rice tradition: 'nara chameshi' (奈良茶飯), rice cooked with tea and roasted, crushed soybeans, a d

chef_bio.background: Yanagi Chaya was founded in 1902 (Meiji 35) beside Sarusawa Pond, in the shadow of Kofukuji's five-story pagoda in central Nara. It was opened specifically to keep alive Nara's old tea-rice tradition: 'nara chameshi' (奈良茶飯), rice cooked with tea and roasted, crushed soybeans, a dish eaten in Nara since ancient times that had been fading from memory. The shop occupies a wooden building that has stood since the Meiji era, and visitors are seated in tatami rooms, at tables, or in private rooms looking out toward the pond.
chef_bio.philosophy: Preserving Nara's tea-rice culture so that it would not be forgotten, served in a historic wooden tea house overlooking Sarusawa Pond.
chef_bio.specialty: Warabi mochi (bracken-starch jelly served with matcha) is the flagship, available year-round; there is also a milk warabi mochi variation with red bean and chestnut, and seasonal kakigori (shaved ice with strawberry or Uji kinako). The founding signature is the nara chameshi set.

anecdotes.text: The founder opened the tea house in 1902 to ensure Nara's tea rice, made from tea and roasted crushed soybeans, would not disappear from the city's table.
The setting beside Sarusawa Pond is considered scenic enough to be worth the visit on its own, with views toward Kofukuji's pagoda.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Shinise.tv confirms a 1902 (Meiji 35) founding beside Sarusawa Pond near Kofukuji's five-story pagoda, opened to preserve nara-chameshi (tea-and-roasted-soybean rice); Meiji-era wooden building with tatami/table/private-room seating; warabi mochi flagship, milk warabi mochi with red bean and chestnut, and strawberry/Uji-kinako kakigori.

positives.text: The signature warabi mochi is made from bracken starch (warabiko), a naturally wheat-free base, served with matcha.

cultural_comfort.note: A relaxed, tourist-familiar traditional tea house by Sarusawa Pond where a friendly greeting and pointing at the warabi mochi or matcha set will get you served comfortably even with limited Japanese.

nara_amenokaku_coffee.gf_detail: Not a gluten-free destination. The signature food is in-house-baked 食パン (wheat shokupan) toast, and there are no documented gluten-free items or celiac accommodations. Plain black coffee is naturally gluten-free, but the kitchen is bread-focused, so this is not celiac-safe.
nara_amenokaku_coffee.vegan_detail: No documented vegan menu. Black filter coffee and the water-diluted BLACK espresso are incidentally plant-based, but the WHITE drink uses steamed milk and the signature toast uses wheat bread with butter/honey toppings. A vegan can drink black coffee but has no documented vegan food option; confirm with staff.
nara_amenokaku_coffee.hours_raw: Official site: 7:00–17:00 (Naramachi main shop). Opening interview / local guides: 7:00–15:00 with irregular closures. Tabelog lists 12:00–17:00 closed Friday. Hours appear to vary, so confirm before visiting.
nara_amenokaku_coffee.notes: [Mom & Pop] 天迦久珈琲 opened on March 1, 2021 in Nara's historic Naramachi district. The founder, Yui Kitaguchi, was 27 at opening and is a licensed English-speaking tour guide who had lived and taught English in English-speaking countries before returning to open the café.

chef_bio.background: 天迦久珈琲 opened on March 1, 2021 in Nara's historic Naramachi district (Nakashinya-cho). The founder, Yui Kitaguchi, was 27 at opening and is a licensed English-speaking interpreter guide who had lived and taught English abroad before returning to open the café.
chef_bio.philosophy: The name 天迦久 (Amenokaku) comes from a deity in the Kojiki who overcomes hardship; the owner chose it hoping to surpass whatever difficulties lie ahead. She washes green beans before roasting for cleanliness and uses spring water from Tenkawa village for brewing, prizing the iron-cast Old Probat roaster for the deep sweetness and flavor it brings out.
chef_bio.specialty: Self-roasted specialty coffee served three ways: WHITE (espresso with steamed milk), BLACK (concentrated espresso), and FILTER (hand drip), each around 550 yen; plus thick toast made from house-baked shokupan, topped with Nara-prefecture honey or peanut butter. Beans are roasted on a 1996 Old Probat machine.

anecdotes.text: The owner is a licensed English-interpreter guide who runs weekday English-conversation café sessions (from mid-afternoon) to help the local community welcome international visitors.
The shop logo was designed by Ouka, a calligraphy artist known for yokai-themed work and an official Nara tourism ambassador.
Beans are roasted on a 1996 Old Probat machine, prized because the iron casting brings out stronger sweetness and flavor than modern equipment.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Nara.keizai.biz and narakko confirm a Mar 1, 2021 opening in Naramachi by Yui Kitaguchi (27), an interpreter-guide who taught English abroad; the Kojiki-derived name; pre-roast bean washing; Tenkawa spring water; a prized 1996 German Old Probat roaster; WHITE/BLACK/FILTER coffees ~550 yen and house-shokupan toast; Ouka-designed logo; and weekday (from ~3pm) English-conversation café sessions.

gf_cross_contamination.text: The café bakes its own wheat shokupan in-house and serves it as toast, so flour and gluten are present on-site; no gluten-free preparation is documented.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Milk is used for the WHITE espresso drink and butter/honey for the toast; no documented separation for vegan orders.

positives.text: The owner is a licensed English-speaking guide, so dietary questions can be asked directly in English.

cultural_comfort.note: The owner is a licensed English-speaking guide who has lived and taught abroad and has run weekend English-conversation café sessions, so a foreign student should feel very comfortable here.

nara_nara_omotenashi_shokudo.gf_detail: No gluten-free program is advertised. This is a Japanese teishoku-style kitchen; menus include sixteen-grain rice, soup and various vegetable preparations that in Japan typically rely on soy sauce and dashi (both common gluten sources via wheat-based soy sauce and fish-stock seasonings). There is no documented dedicated gluten-free menu, no stated cross-contamination controls, and a shared home-style kitchen, so a celiac traveler should not assume safety and would need to ask directly about every dish, including the soy sauce and stock used.
nara_nara_omotenashi_shokudo.vegan_detail: The signature からだ想いベジプレート (body-kind vegetable plate, ~1,650 yen) is a meat-free, monthly-changing plate of about eight vegetable dishes with roughly 350g of vegetables (e.g. lentil salad, samosa-style potato gyoza, simmered kombu, daikon-and-hijiki, marinades, a detox soup, sixteen-grain rice). It is explicitly meat-free, but there is no published confirmation that it is fully vegan: Japanese vegetable simmered dishes and soups very commonly use fish dashi (bonito/katsuo) and the gyoza/田楽 components may contain non-vegan seasonings. The rest of the menu features meat- and fish-based plates. A vegan diner should confirm dashi, fish products and egg/dairy in each component before ordering.
nara_nara_omotenashi_shokudo.notes: A small individually-run cafe-restaurant a short walk from Kintetsu Nara Station, reached by heading down the Konishi-dori arcade and crossing Sanjo-dori. It built its identity around home-style cooking you can eat with confidence every day.

chef_bio.background: A small individually-run cafe-restaurant about a three-minute walk from Kintetsu Nara Station, reached by heading down the Konishi-dori arcade and crossing Sanjo-dori. It built its identity around home-style cooking you can eat with confidence every day.
chef_bio.philosophy: Built on the idea of 'homemade, body-kind food you can eat with peace of mind every day,' emphasizing generous vegetables and nutritional balance.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature dish is the からだ想いベジプレート (body-kind vegetable plate), a monthly-rotating, meat-free plate of about eight vegetable dishes with roughly 350g of vegetables served with sixteen-grain rice. The kitchen also serves meat- and fish-centered plates, healthy curries, and takeout bento.

anecdotes.text: The interior is finished with a generous amount of hinoki cypress grown in Nara Prefecture, giving the counter, table and terrace seating a bright, warm feel.

The vegetable plate changes monthly and has featured items such as lentil salad, samosa-style potato gyoza, simmered kombu, shredded daikon with hijiki, eggplant-and-tomato marinade, and a spring-cabbage and yuzu-pepper detox soup.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Nara-gourmet confirms an owner-run 'homemade, body-kind everyday food' cafe 3 min from Kintetsu Nara (via Konishi-dori, past Sanjo-dori), whose signature monthly-rotating vegetable plate has ~8 dishes and ~350g veg with 16-grain rice, alongside protein plates, healthy curries and takeout bento, in a Nara-hinoki interior with counter/table/terrace seating.

positives.text: Offers a clearly meat-free vegetable plate with around 350g of vegetables across roughly eight dishes, making it an easy choice for diners avoiding meat.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, calm individually-run teishoku spot where a little spoken Japanese will help you order and ask about ingredients, though pointing at the vegetable plate works in a pinch.

nara_oyatsuya_323_oyatsuya_mi.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. The entire lineup is wheat-flour baked goods — canelés, financiers, madeleines, Breton galettes, scones, and butter sandwich cookies — so it is unsuitable for celiac or gluten-avoiding diners. No gluten-free items are documented.
nara_oyatsuya_323_oyatsuya_mi.vegan_detail: Not vegan. The baked goods are built around cultured butter, eggs, and dairy (financiers with browned butter, butter-rich Breton galettes, butter sandwich cookies); no vegan items are documented.
nara_oyatsuya_323_oyatsuya_mi.notes: [Mom & Pop] OYATSUYA 323 (おやつや みつみ) opened on November 1, 2022, in a quiet back alley off the Mochiidono shopping street in Nara's old-town Naramachi district. It is a tiny one-shop sweets atelier run by a pastry chef who previously trained and worked at prestigious hotels, including the Imp

chef_bio.background: OYATSUYA 323 (おやつや みつみ) opened on November 1, 2022, in a quiet back alley off the Mochiidono shopping street in Nara's old-town Naramachi district. It is a tiny one-shop sweets atelier run by a pastry chef who previously trained and worked at prestigious hotels, including the Imperial Hotel Osaka and a JW Marriott property, before setting out to open a small neighborhood bakery of their own.
chef_bio.philosophy: A small, approachable neighborhood okashi shop that pairs serious hotel-trained pastry technique with a sense of humor, seen in playful pun-named items like the sea-bream (medetai) butter sandwich cookie.
chef_bio.specialty: French-style baked confections: rum-and-vanilla canelés with a crisp shell and chewy center, almond browned-butter financiers made with cultured butter, thick rum-scented Breton galettes, bite-size 'scrap' scones (plain, chocolate, Earl Grey), and playful sea-bream-shaped butter sandwich cookies filled with red bean and butter.

anecdotes.text: The owner is a pastry chef with a hotel background (Imperial Hotel Osaka, JW Marriott) who chose a narrow Naramachi side street to open their own small okashi shop.
Signature items include a large rum-and-vanilla canelé with a crisp exterior and chewy interior, and a sea-bream-shaped butter sandwich cookie filled with red bean and butter.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Nara-gourmet confirms a Nov 1, 2022 opening in a Mochiidono/Naramachi back alley by a hotel-trained (Imperial Hotel Osaka, JW Marriott) pastry chef; signatures include rum-vanilla canelé, cultured-butter almond financier, rum Breton galette, plain/chocolate/Earl Grey scrap scones, and a pun-on-'medetai' sea-bream butter sandwich cookie with red bean and butter.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Everything sold is wheat-flour baked goods made in the same small kitchen, so cross-contact with gluten is unavoidable throughout the shop.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Items are made with butter, eggs and dairy; no separation from animal products is documented.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny, casual counter sweets shop where you can simply point at the baked goods you want, making it very easy for a foreign student even with no Japanese.

nara_afternoon_tea_rocher.gf_detail: This is an afternoon tea specialist built around wheat-based pastries, scones, quiche/pies, cakes and petit fours, so it is not suitable for celiacs or strict gluten-free diets. There is no documented gluten-free menu, dedicated equipment, or allergen handling. A gluten-free traveler would have essentially nothing safe to eat here.
nara_afternoon_tea_rocher.vegan_detail: The set menu centers on dairy, eggs and cured meat: butter-based scones and pastries, Mont Blanc, meringue, nougat glacé, prosciutto cake salé and anchovy/fish pie, plus quiche. Nothing in the documented menu is vegan and there is no stated vegan option, though some plant-forward items (carrot salad, Nara-vegetable elements) exist. A vegan should ask in advance; expect very limited or no suitable options.
nara_afternoon_tea_rocher.hours_raw: Mon/Tue/Wed/Fri/Sat/Sun 12:00-17:00 (food L.O. 15:00) / closed Thu. Some sources give weekdays 12:00-15:30 and weekends/holidays until around 16:00. 90-minute time limit.
nara_afternoon_tea_rocher.notes: Owner-pastry chef Iwasaki trained at well-regarded patisseries in Tokyo, Fukuoka, Paris and Normandy before building a string of beloved Nara dessert spots, including the patisserie Bon Chic, Patisserie Karaku, the Taiwanese sweets shop Sarusawa Touka, and Cheesecake Rocks. He is

chef_bio.background: Owner-pastry chef Iwasaki trained at well-regarded patisseries in Tokyo, Fukuoka, Paris and Normandy before building a string of beloved Nara dessert spots, including the patisserie Bon Chic, Patisserie Karaku, the Taiwanese sweets shop Sarusawa Touka, and Cheesecake Rocks. He is also a certified tea advisor and personally curates the tea list.
chef_bio.philosophy: A fusion of Japanese and Western aesthetics inside a century-old machiya, offering an accessible luxury: a full, professionally made afternoon tea from around ¥3,400, in a setting that warmly welcomes solo guests rather than requiring groups.
chef_bio.specialty: Three-tier afternoon tea built on Nara-prefecture ingredients: savories like prosciutto cake salé, anchovy fish pie and Nara-vegetable quiche; scones made with local hōjicha and Yamato tea with chocolate chips and local honey; and petit fours such as pumpkin-caramel tart, Mont Blanc, strawberry-rose-chocolate tart, champagne biscuit and matcha meringue.

anecdotes.text: The cafe occupies a machiya over 100 years old in the Naramachi district; the building previously housed a cafe called 'Naramachi-mura,' and Iwasaki took it over through a connection with the former owner, preserving original wooden beams and pillars while adding William Morris-style wallpaper, European antiques and a preserved tatami tea room. The name 'Rocher' is French for 'rock,' a nod to his surname.

The tea program features Nara producers and a touch of history: award-winning 'Tsuki no Kaori' black tea from Tea Farm Inokura, premium Yamato hōjicha from Kenichi Shizen Noen, and a Naramachi masala chai blended with a long-established Kikuoka kanpo (herbal) apothecary, alongside German Ronnefeldt teas.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Rurubu confirms owner-chef Iwasaki (岩崎能久), trained in Tokyo/Fukuoka/Paris/Normandy, a JSFCA tea advisor, in a 100+ yr Naramachi machiya formerly the 'Naramachi-mura' cafe, with Morris wallpaper/European antiques/tatami room and the 'Rocher'=rock surname nod. Narakko confirms his prior Nara shops (Bon Chic, Patisserie Karaku, Sarusawa Touka, Cheesecake Rocks) and the Nara-producer tea list (Yamato black tea, hojicha, Kikuoka masala chai).

gf_cross_contamination.text: The entire menu is built on wheat (scones, pastries, cakes, quiche, pies, biscuits), so cross-contamination is inherent and the venue is not suitable for celiacs. No gluten-free handling is documented.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Dishes are prepared with shared dairy, eggs and meat (prosciutto, anchovy); no vegan preparation or separation is documented.

positives.text: Menu items and ingredients (Nara-vegetable quiche, carrot salad, prosciutto cake salé, anchovy fish pie, local-tea scones, named petit fours) are described in detail by published articles, helping diners identify what they are eating, though no formal allergen program is documented.

cultural_comfort.note: A foreign student would find a warm welcome to solo diners but should expect a primarily Japanese-language setting and reservations made by phone or Instagram DM, so a little Japanese (or a translation app) helps.

nara_soba_dokoro_kinose_2.gf_detail: Not gluten-free safe. The dipping sauce (tsuyu) is made with soy sauce, which contains wheat, and even the 100% buckwheat (jūwari) soba is prepared in a kitchen handling wheat-based two-eight (nihachi) soba and tempura, so cross-contamination is highly likely. No celiac accommodation is documented.
nara_soba_dokoro_kinose_2.vegan_detail: Not vegan-friendly. Soba broth is based on fish dashi (bonito/kombu), and most dishes involve fish, egg (e.g. soft-boiled egg soba), or tempura. No documented vegan options.
nara_soba_dokoro_kinose_2.hours_raw: Mon, Wed-Sun & holidays 11:00-14:30; closed Tuesdays. (An older local-guide listing also showed a 17:00-20:00 dinner service with Tuesday and Friday evening closed, but current Tabelog/Gnavi listings show lunch only.)
nara_soba_dokoro_kinose_2.notes: [Mom & Pop] A small, intimate hand-made soba shop tucked into the historic Naramachi district, directly in front of the Naramachi Center and a short stroll from Sarusawa Pond. It blends a traditional townhouse setting of table and tatami seating with a quietly modern touch, with jazz playing

chef_bio.background: A small, intimate hand-made soba shop tucked into the historic Naramachi district, directly in front of the Naramachi Center and a short stroll from Sarusawa Pond. It blends a traditional townhouse setting of table and tatami seating with a quietly modern touch, with jazz playing softly in the dining room.
chef_bio.philosophy: An emphasis on craftsmanship and quality ingredients, pairing carefully made soba with sake and shochu for an unhurried soba-shop drink before the meal.
chef_bio.specialty: Hand-cut soba made from 100% domestic buckwheat flour and natural spring water. The house standard is a refined nihachi (two-eight) soba served with a Kanto-style broth; a pure 100% buckwheat (jūwari) version is available for a +100 yen supplement. Signature plates include soba topped with soft-boiled onsen egg and tempura bits (agedama), grated-yam tororo soba, and soba set meals, and diners are invited to taste the noodles with a pinch of salt.

anecdotes.text: The shop sits right in front of the Naramachi Center and plays jazz in the background, mixing table and tatami seating for a calm, refined atmosphere.
Noodles are made from 100% domestic buckwheat flour and natural spring water, with a pure 100% buckwheat option offered alongside the standard two-eight blend.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: nara-gourmet.com states the shop is directly in front of Naramachi Center with jazz and table/tatami seating; noodles use 100% domestic buckwheat flour and natural spring water, standard nihachi with jūwari available for +100 yen, Kanto-style tsuyu, onsen-egg/agedama and tororo soba, and a salt tasting.

gf_cross_contamination.text: The kitchen prepares both 100% buckwheat soba and wheat-containing two-eight (nihachi) soba plus tempura, so even the jūwari soba is highly likely to share equipment and water with wheat products.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Soba is served with a Kanto-style broth/dipping sauce based on soy sauce, which contains wheat.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broth is fish-dashi based and the menu includes egg and tempura dishes; no vegan-dedicated preparation is documented.

positives.text: Diners may eat the soba with a pinch of salt instead of sauce, which avoids the wheat-containing broth (though the noodles themselves are not certified gluten-free).

cultural_comfort.note: A relaxed neighborhood soba shop where a friendly greeting and pointing at the menu will get you by, though staff likely speak limited English.

But essentially a single self-claim with no celiac-grade corroboration of actual GF handling; an aggregator review even doubts the claim ('I'm not sure their gluten-free claim is true'). Fails ≥2-source 'high'. — Prior note: The kitchen states it uses no wheat in its dishes and describes itself as "添加物・グルテン不使用" (additive- and gluten-free). The staple is organic sprouted brown rice, which can also be eaten as house-made gluten-free brown rice noodles (玄米麺), served cold in spring/summer. This is a genuinely wheat-avoiding, grain-conscious kitchen, so it is strong for gluten-free diners. However, it is not explicitly described as a certified celiac-safe facility and no dedicated-equipment / cross-contamination protocol is documented, so a strict celiac should still confirm by phone (Japanese) before visiting.
nara_kururu_2.vegan_detail: The cafe's menus are made without fish, meat, dairy, or wheat, with carefully selected grains and vegetables and minimal additives/pesticides — explicitly described as suitable for people practicing veganism. The signature tofu hamburger plate (豆腐ハンバーグプレート) comes with pre-meal shiso tea, the tofu patty with carrot puree, small side dishes, salad, sprouted brown rice, and miso soup, all plant-based. This is a genuinely vegan kitchen, not an omnivore place with a few options.
nara_kururu_2.hours_raw: Tabelog lists 09:00-21:30 (L.O. 21:00). Official site reception hours: 10:00-18:00. Hours vary by season and reservation status.

chef_bio.background: KURURU is a natural-food cafe (billed as a 'Total Therapy Cafe Salon') on the second floor of the Inoue Building along the Higashimuki shopping arcade, about a 2-minute walk from Kintetsu Nara Station. The owner developed the menu through independent research into therapeutic, plant-based eating, and the cafe bills itself as Japan's first food-therapy specialty house — the idea of 'eating fasting' (食べるファスティング), where simple, clean dishes nourish and gently cleanse at the same time.
chef_bio.philosophy: Cooking is kept simple to draw out the natural umami of the ingredients, prioritizing Nara-grown produce and carefully chosen seasonings while going additive- and gluten-free, with menus made to accommodate vegan, vegetarian, allergy and dietary-therapy needs. The owner frames mindful, lighter eating as a small contribution toward the SDGs.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature dish is the tofu hamburger plate (豆腐ハンバーグプレート): the shop's No.1 tofu patty with carrot puree, served with a pre-meal shiso tea, three small side dishes, salad, sprouted brown rice, and seasonal-vegetable miso soup. The kitchen also makes its own gluten-free organic brown-rice noodles (玄米麺), plus handmade sweets like banana cake.

anecdotes.text: KURURU operates as a 'Total Therapy Cafe Salon,' pairing the food with a wellness salon offering aroma and stone-body therapy, footbaths, and healing yoga — reflecting its whole-body approach to food and health.
Its house-developed gluten-free brown-rice noodles are popular enough to be sold for nationwide delivery beyond the cafe itself.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Official site calls KURURU Japan's first food-therapy shop with additive- and gluten-free 'edible fasting'; nara-gourmet details the No.1 tofu-hamburger plate (carrot puree, shiso pre-meal tea, 3 sides, sprouted brown rice, miso soup), vegan/vegetarian/allergy support, and self-developed brown-rice noodles sold nationwide; Hot Pepper Beauty confirms the co-located Total Therapy salon with aroma, footbath and yoga.

staff_allergy_handling.text: The owner has independently researched and developed vegan, vegetarian, and allergen-conscious dishes, indicating awareness of dietary needs (no documented formal protocol).

positives.text: All menus are prepared without fish, meat, dairy, or wheat, using carefully selected grains and vegetables with minimal additives and pesticides.
The kitchen describes its food as additive- and gluten-free (添加物・グルテン不使用), built around organic sprouted brown rice and house-made brown-rice noodles.
positives.source_wording: Current site (renewed 2026-06-15): 「全国初のフードセラピー専門店。独自研究から生まれた『食べるファスティング』は添加物・グルテン不使用で、循環や巡りを良くし…」

positives.text: The signature tofu hamburger plate is explicitly noted as suitable for people practicing veganism.

cultural_comfort.note: A calm, owner-run natural-food cafe where a friendly greeting and pointing at the popular tofu hamburger plate will get you far, though menu explanations are mostly in Japanese so a translation app helps.

But essentially a single self-claim with no celiac-grade corroboration of actual GF handling; an aggregator review even doubts the claim ('I'm not sure their gluten-free claim is true'). Fails ≥2-source 'high'.
red_flags: Only the venue asserts GF safety; no independent celiac-grade corroboration
A reviewer explicitly doubts the GF claim
Shared kitchen (vegan + salon/studio); no documented dedicated prep/CC
Miso soup (barley) and curry roux (normally wheat) claimed GF but unverifiable
gf_review.plain_rice: Partial — sprouted brown-rice + brown-rice onigiri exist (white rice not confirmed); miso soup itself a trap. Use brown-rice balls, confirm no soy seasoning.

nara_edogawa_naramachi.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. The signature kabayaki tare (sauce) used on every eel dish is a soy-sauce/mirin-based glaze, and Japanese soy sauce normally contains wheat; rice bowls are served with this sauce. Side dishes and set components also use soy-based seasonings and dashi. No gluten-free menu, labeling, or dedicated preparation is documented, so this is not safe for celiacs.
nara_edogawa_naramachi.vegan_detail: This is a specialist eel restaurant. The core of the menu is unagi (eel) served as unaju/unadon and hitsumabushi, all built on a fish-based kabayaki tare and rice. Set meals and side dishes rely on fish dashi and animal proteins. There is no documented vegan or vegetarian menu, and nothing here is suitable for a strict plant-based diet.
nara_edogawa_naramachi.hours_raw: Mon-Fri 11:00-15:00, 17:00-21:00; Sat-Sun 11:00-21:00. Closed the 3rd Thursday of each month.
nara_edogawa_naramachi.notes: The restaurant occupies a roughly 150-year-old former merchant house in the heart of Naramachi. Built in the early Meiji era and later home to the Miyajima family, it operated for generations as a kimono and textile shop—its latticed itoya-goshi facade still signals that fiber-tr

chef_bio.background: The restaurant occupies a roughly 150-year-old former merchant house in the heart of Naramachi. Built in the Meiji era, it was owned by the Miyajima family, who ran a kimono and textile shop here for generations—its latticed itoya-goshi facade still signals that fiber-trade past. After the shop closed in 1985, the building was carefully converted into a dining house, keeping original details such as a wooden box-staircase (hakodansu) that is still in use, along with sunken-hearth-style seating.
chef_bio.philosophy: The kitchen follows the old eel-cook's creed, 'three years to skewer, eight years to fillet, a lifetime to grill,' and continually replenishes a founding tare said to carry more than seventy years of accumulated flavor.
chef_bio.specialty: Tokyo (Kanto)-style eel: the fish is split along the back, skewered and white-grilled, then steamed to render out fat and finished with a second grill, so it turns soft, fluffy and lighter in fat. Signature dishes include unaju/unadon over rice with a long-aged kabayaki sauce, and hitsumabushi served so you can enjoy it three ways.

anecdotes.text: The neighboring former storehouse, called Kura-no-ma, has been converted into a chic bar used as a quiet space for private gatherings.
The Edo-yaki method—back-splitting, an initial white-grill, steaming to render out fat, then a final grill—is what gives the eel its tender, fluffy texture.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: small-life documents the ~150-yr Meiji building owned by the Miyajima kimono family, closed 1985, with itoya-goshi lattice, a still-functioning hakodansu, sunken-hearth seating, and the former storehouse Kura-no-ma now a chic bar. The official site confirms the 'three years to skewer...' creed, a 70+-year continually-topped tare, back-split/steam/grill preparation, unadon and hitsumabushi.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The eel is finished with a soy-sauce/mirin-based kabayaki tare brushed onto every dish; standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, so the glaze is a gluten source.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Menu is centered on eel and fish-based sauce and dashi throughout; no plant-based preparation is documented.

cultural_comfort.note: A polished but welcoming eel restaurant where a foreign student can order comfortably by pointing at picture menus and saying a few words of Japanese; English support is not guaranteed, so a translation app helps.

nara_cafe_haru.gf_detail: Not gluten-free friendly. The core menu (baked curry with curry roux, pasta, gratin/doria, cream croquettes, breaded cutlets, dessert plates) is wheat-heavy, and no gluten-free accommodation is documented. Not safe for celiacs.
nara_cafe_haru.vegan_detail: Not vegan-friendly. Signature dishes center on shrimp, beef/pork hamburger, roast beef, chicken nanban, and cheese; the tomato cream pasta sauce reportedly uses sakura-shrimp paste, bonito, and kelp. No vegan options are documented.
nara_cafe_haru.hours_raw: 11:00-15:30 (L.O.); some sources list 11:00-15:00 or until ingredients sell out

chef_bio.background: Cafe Haru is the third venture (3号店) of the well-loved, Michelin-listed Western-style restaurant Yoshoku Haru, set inside a renovated traditional Naramachi townhouse with red lattice work and vintage furnishings that echo the area's old pleasure-district character. It opened in October 2017, a short two-to-three-minute walk from its perpetually busy original location, offering a calmer place to sit during a stroll through the historic district. Owner-chef Daiki Nakabayashi, who cooks with a prosthetic arm, hails from Kitakyushu.
chef_bio.philosophy: Bringing a hometown specialty to Nara: the owner, who is from Kitakyushu/Moji where baked curry is a local signature, recreates that dish in a comfortable townhouse setting with generous, good-value portions.
chef_bio.specialty: Baked curry (yaki curry) — especially the shrimp baked curry, served sizzling in a deep iron pot with crispy rice, beef curry, melted mozzarella, a soft egg, and grilled prawns; also tomato cream pasta with tiger prawns, stewed Yamato-beef-and-pork hamburger, chicken nanban, and dessert plates.

anecdotes.text: The owner hails from Kitakyushu/Moji, where baked curry is one of the region's signature dishes, and brought that specialty to his Naramachi cafe.
Positioned as a less-crowded alternative just a couple of minutes from the always-busy original Yoshoku Haru, while sharing the same culinary identity.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: naramogu identifies Cafe Haru as the 3号店 of Yoshoku Haru, run by Kitakyushu-born chef Daiki Nakabayashi (who has a prosthetic arm), 2-3 min from the original, with shrimp baked curry as the top item; nara-gourmet/naramachiinfo confirm the renovated townhouse and Moji-origin baked curry; a Sankei article records the October 2017 opening (packed on day one).

vegan_cross_contact.text: The tomato cream pasta sauce is reported to combine sakura-shrimp paste, bonito, and kelp, and signature dishes feature shrimp, beef/pork, and cheese, so animal products are central to the kitchen.

cultural_comfort.note: A relaxed local townhouse cafe where a foreign student can comfortably point at the signature baked curry on a picture menu, though staff communication is mainly in Japanese.

nara_chagayu_salon_tsukihibos.gf_detail: The core meal is rice-based: freshly cooked chagayu (rice simmered in tea), white rice, and a buffet of 20+ pickled Yamato vegetables, which is naturally a more rice-forward, low-wheat spread than most Japanese restaurants. However there is no gluten-free program, no labeling, and no dedicated handling. Many Japanese pickles are seasoned with soy sauce (which usually contains wheat), and the miso soup most likely uses standard miso/dashi. A celiac visitor cannot assume any specific dish is safe and would need to ask, in Japanese, which pickles avoid soy sauce/wheat. Treat as not verified celiac-safe.
nara_chagayu_salon_tsukihibos.vegan_detail: The format is vegetable-forward: rice, chagayu and 20+ pickled seasonal Yamato vegetables, so a largely plant-based plate is achievable. But the restaurant makes no vegan claim. Some pickles may be cured with bonito (katsuo) or other fish-derived seasonings, and the miso soup most likely uses fish dashi, so it is not a verified vegan venue. A vegan can probably build a satisfying plate from the pickle and rice buffet but should ask which pickles are free of fish/bonito and skip the miso soup.
nara_chagayu_salon_tsukihibos.hours_raw: 11:00-16:00 (irregular days off) - Tabelog lists kitchen/serving to 15:30

chef_bio.background: A small, independent cafe-restaurant set right by Nara Park, between the Nara National Museum and Himuro Shrine on Noborioji-dori, a roughly 10-minute walk from Kintetsu Nara Station toward Todai-ji. It celebrates one of Nara's oldest everyday foods, chagayu (rice slowly simmered in tea), pairing it with the region's deep pickling tradition.
chef_bio.philosophy: The place leans into Nara's identity as a city of pickles and tea porridge, letting guests graze slowly through many small vegetable pickles rather than ordering a single fixed plate.
chef_bio.specialty: An all-you-can-eat spread built around freshly cooked chagayu and Nara-grown rice, served with a buffet of more than 20 carefully chosen pickles made from seasonal Yamato (Nara) vegetables, plus miso soup, roasted tea and house-made monaka, all refillable.

anecdotes.text: The dining room is a bright, open space hung with photographs of Nara's temples, shrines and Buddha statues, and there is a garden terrace where you can eat in the green shade of trees said to be several hundred years old; it is also pet-friendly.

Local Nara guide Narakko describes it as a spot to enjoy Nara's local chagayu with a pickle buffet of 20-plus seasonal prefectural-vegetable pickles, freshly cooked chagayu and local rice, and refillable house-made sweets.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The official about page describes a shop beside Nara Park serving all-you-can-eat chagayu with Nara rice and a buffet of 20+ curated seasonal Yamato-vegetable pickles, miso soup, roasted tea and house monaka (all refillable), a bright room hung with temple/Buddha photos, a garden terrace under several-hundred-year-old trees, and pet-friendly dining.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The meal centers on many small vegetable pickles; Japanese pickles are commonly seasoned with soy sauce, which usually contains wheat, and the menu provides no wheat/gluten labeling.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Some Nara-style pickles can be cured with bonito or other fish-derived seasonings, and the accompanying miso soup most likely uses fish dashi, so a strict vegan should confirm which pickles are fish-free and skip the soup.

positives.text: The format is buffet-style with rice, tea porridge and 20-plus vegetable pickles you serve yourself, so it is easy to build a vegetable-and-rice plate and to see what you are taking.

cultural_comfort.note: A relaxed buffet-style spot where you can serve yourself rice, chagayu and pickles, so a foreign student gets by fine with a friendly konnichiwa and gestures, though staff communication is mostly in Japanese and it is cash only.
